## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sumaṅgalajātaka* (Ja 420) is a canonical birth tale belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali Tipiṭaka. According to its traditional framing story, the Buddha related this account while residing at Jetavana to provide an admonition to a king, telling the tale of the past at the monarch's request and opening with the line “Conscious of an angry frown”. The narrative conveys principles of governance and justice free from wrath; in modern studies of Buddhist ethics, verses from the Jātaka are highlighted as evidence of Buddhism's rejection of righteous indignation and retributive anger, asserting that any necessary chastisement must proceed from compassion rather than hatred: “Anger shall not check my bent: / When to vice I take the sword, / Pity prompts the punishment” [Goodman 2009].
